title: Given a set of words and a typed prefix, return all words that start with that prefix, optionally limited to the top few. Explain how the Trie pattern provides autocomplete, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Autocomplete Suggestions (Return Words Matching a Typed Prefix)

s1_definition.profdef: Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie pattern. We insert all words into a trie, walk down to the node at the end of the typed prefix, then run a depth-first search from that node to gather every completed word beneath it. Reaching the prefix node costs the prefix length, and gathering suggestions costs time proportional to the matching subtree.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India offers a search box where a teller types the start of a payee name and the system instantly suggests all registered payees beginning with those letters. A trie walks straight to the typed prefix and collects every name underneath it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk to the prefix node, then collect every word in the subtree below it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie pattern. We insert all words into a trie, walk down to the node at the end of the typed prefix, then run a depth-first search from that node to gather every completed word beneath it. Reaching the prefix node costs the prefix length, and gathering suggestions costs time proportional to the matching subtree.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India offers a search box where a teller types the start of a payee name and the system instantly suggests all registered payees beginning with those letters. A trie walks straight to the typed prefix and collects every name underneath it.

**One line to remember:** Walk to the prefix node, then collect every word in the subtree below it.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a trie of all words, marking each word end. To autocomplete a prefix we first walk from the root following the prefix characters. If any character has no matching child, no word starts with the prefix and we return an empty list. Otherwise we arrive at the prefix node, and every complete word stored in the subtree rooted there is a valid suggestion. We run a depth-first search from that node, building up the suffix as we descend and recording a full word each time we pass a node marked as a word end.

The collection core is `void collect(TrieNode node, StringBuilder cur, List<String> out, int limit) { if (out.size() >= limit) return; if (node.isWord) out.add(cur.toString()); for (var e : node.children.entrySet()) { cur.append(e.getKey()); collect(e.getValue(), cur, out, limit); cur.deleteCharAt(cur.length() - 1); } }`. Visiting children in sorted order yields alphabetical suggestions, and an early return enforces a top-few limit. A concrete check: with payees RAJESH, RAJIV, PRIYA and prefix RAJ, the suggestions are RAJESH and RAJIV. Senior nuance: reaching the prefix node is order of the prefix length, gathering is proportional to the matched subtree, and for very large tries each node can cache its top suggestions to answer instantly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India provides a payee search box where a teller types the first few letters of a registered payee name and expects an instant list of all matching payees, limited to a handful of top suggestions. Scanning the full payee list on every keystroke does not scale. This is exactly how Autocomplete Suggestions works: it walks a trie to the typed prefix and collects the matching payee names beneath it.

The code defines a `PayeeAutocompleteService` with `suggest(prefix, limit)` and `insert(name)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` inserts a few payee names and logs the suggestions for a prefix.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the payee set RAJESH, RAJIV, PRIYA, with the typed prefix RAJ and a limit of five.

Step 1 — We build the trie, so RAJESH and RAJIV share the R, A, J branch and then split at E and I, while PRIYA sits on its own P branch.

Step 2 — We walk the prefix RAJ from the root: R has a child, A has a child, J has a child, so we arrive at the J node successfully.

Step 3 — From the J node we run a depth-first collection, descending in alphabetical order. The E branch completes RAJESH, which we record first.

Step 4 — Back at the J node we take the I branch, which completes RAJIV, which we record second. The PRIYA name is on a different branch and is never reached from the RAJ prefix node.

Step 5 — The limit of five is not reached, so both suggestions are returned in alphabetical order as RAJESH and RAJIV. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 10:08:04 PM com.bank.payeeac.service.PayeeAutocompleteService suggest
INFO: Suggestions for RAJ = [RAJESH, RAJIV]
Oct 27, 2026 10:08:04 PM com.bank.payeeac.PayeeAutocompleteApplication main
INFO: Autocomplete for RAJ: [RAJESH, RAJIV]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Insert RAJESH, RAJIV, PRIYA
    │ root → R→A→J ─┬─ E→S→H(isWord RAJESH)
    │               └─ I→V(isWord RAJIV)
    │ root → P→R→I→Y→A(isWord PRIYA)
    ▼
  suggest("RAJ", 5): walk R,A,J → prefix node
    │ collect subtree alphabetically (limit 5)
    │ E-branch → RAJESH ; I-branch → RAJIV
    ▼
  Output: [RAJESH, RAJIV]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie pattern, and I describe it in two clean phases. First I insert all the words into a trie and mark each word end, then to autocomplete a typed prefix I walk from the root following the prefix characters. If any character has no matching child, nothing starts with that prefix and I return an empty list. Otherwise I arrive at the prefix node, and every complete word stored in the subtree beneath that node is a valid suggestion.

The second phase is a depth-first search from the prefix node, building up the suffix as I descend and recording a full word each time I pass a node marked as a word end. If I store the children in sorted order the suggestions come out alphabetically, and an early return once I have gathered enough enforces a top-few limit. Reaching the prefix node costs time proportional to the prefix length, and gathering the suggestions costs time proportional to the matched subtree, which is exactly why a trie powers fast autocomplete.

At the National Bank of India I used this behind a payee search box where a teller typed the first few letters of a registered payee name and expected an instant list of matching payees. I warmed the trie from the database, served keystrokes from memory, and cached hot prefixes in Redis. Explaining the walk-to-prefix-then-collect-subtree structure, the alphabetical ordering from sorted children, and the limit through an early return is what shows an interviewer I understand this prefix-collection use of the Trie pattern.
